look_alikes: False Morel, Verpa bohemica
habitat_notes: Disturbed woods, burn edges, orchards, and cottonwood corridors
range_notes: A spring mushroom recognized by a pitted cap and a single hollow interior, with dangerous false-morel confusion to rule out.
notes: Toxic raw or undercooked. False morels can cause severe poisoning.

look_alikes: Bitter Bolete, Red-pored boletes
habitat_notes: Conifer and mixed forest, often at montane elevations
range_notes: A stout, brown-capped bolete with pale pores and fine white netting on the upper stem.
notes: Skip boletes with red or orange pores or strong blue bruising until an expert has ruled out toxic species.

look_alikes: False Chanterelle, Jack-o'-lantern, Woolly Chanterelle
habitat_notes: Moist spruce and other conifer forest
range_notes: A western chanterelle with blunt forked ridges, solid pale flesh, and a young pinkish cap bloom.
notes: True gills or growth in dense clusters on wood point away from chanterelles and toward possible toxic lookalikes.

look_alikes: Old lobster mushroom, Unparasitized Russula or Lactarius
habitat_notes: Conifer and mixed forest floor, often partly buried
range_notes: A firm host mushroom transformed by a red-orange parasitic fungus that erases most of the original gills.
notes: Reject soft, purple-tinged, foul, or badly decayed specimens because the original host can no longer be identified.

look_alikes: Angel Wings, Jack-o'-lantern, Crepidotus species
habitat_notes: Dead or declining hardwood; substrate helps separate similar Pleurotus species
range_notes: Pale fan-shaped caps growing in shelves on wood, with gills descending a short off-center stem.
notes: Confirm the substrate and spore print. Thin white fans on conifer wood may be angel wings, which have been implicated in severe illness.

look_alikes: Common Inky Cap, Green-spored Parasol, Amanita button
habitat_notes: Lawns, trail edges, compacted ground, and other disturbed soil
range_notes: A tall white ink cap whose shaggy cylinder dissolves from the rim into black liquid as it matures.
notes: Only young, all-white specimens are considered edible, and every lawn button should be sliced to rule out an Amanita structure.

look_alikes: Amanita button, Earthball, Mature puffball
habitat_notes: Forest litter, trail edges, and disturbed ground
range_notes: A pear-shaped puffball with detachable cone-shaped spines and a mandatory pure-white slice test.
notes: Slice every specimen top to bottom. Any internal cap, gills, stem, dark center, or yellowing rules it out for eating.

look_alikes: Other Hydnum species, Scaly Hedgehog, Hydnellum species
habitat_notes: Mossy conifer and mixed forest
range_notes: A woodland mushroom with soft detachable teeth under the cap instead of gills or pores.
notes: The toothed group is distinctive, but regional Hydnum taxonomy is complex. Confirm all field marks and local range.

look_alikes: Bear's Head Tooth, Coral Tooth
habitat_notes: Wounds in living hardwoods and fallen hardwood logs
range_notes: A white hardwood fungus formed from one cushion of long dangling teeth, without a cap, gills, or stem.
notes: Supplement claims outpace human evidence. A wild identification and a medicinal claim are separate questions.

look_alikes: Panther Cap, Rain-washed Amanita, Russula species
habitat_notes: Under conifers and birch
range_notes: The iconic red or yellow Amanita with white veil warts, white gills, a ring, and a bulbous base marked by scaly rings.
notes: Poisonous. Muscimol and ibotenic acid products are not a safe shortcut, and ordinary cooking does not make this mushroom safe.

look_alikes: Young Puffball, Meadow Mushroom, White Parasol
habitat_notes: Woodland soil near host trees
range_notes: A deadly white Amanita pattern defined by free white gills, a ring, white spores, and a buried sack-like volva.
notes: Potentially fatal. If ingestion is possible, call Poison Control immediately before symptoms appear.

look_alikes: Morel, Snow Morels, Verpa species
habitat_notes: Conifer forest and disturbed ground
range_notes: A spring mushroom with brain-like folds and a chambered interior that overlaps true-morel habitat and can cause severe poisoning.
notes: Poisonous. The site does not endorse traditional detoxification methods, and cooking fumes have caused illness.

look_alikes: Jack-o'-lantern, Berkeley's Polypore, Black-staining Polypore
habitat_notes: Living or dead hardwood trunks, stumps, and buried roots
range_notes: Bright orange and yellow shelves on wood, with a sulfur-yellow pore surface and no gills.
notes: Regional Laetiporus species and host trees matter. Cook thoroughly and try only a small portion because gastrointestinal reactions occur.

look_alikes: Jack-o'-lantern, False Chanterelle, Rainbow Chanterelle
habitat_notes: Soil in mature broadleaf and conifer forests, depending on region
range_notes: A golden woodland chanterelle with blunt forked ridges, solid pale flesh, and no true gill blades.
notes: Golden chanterelles are a regional species complex. Confirm local taxonomy and rule out orange, gilled mushrooms growing from wood.

look_alikes: Amanita button, Common Earthball, Western Giant Puffball
habitat_notes: Meadows, pasture edges, open woods, parks, and rich disturbed soil
range_notes: A stemless white ball that can grow larger than a basketball and must be cut open before any culinary consideration.
notes: Slice the entire specimen. Edible-stage flesh must be uniformly white with no internal outline, discoloration, or forming cap and gills.

look_alikes: Black-staining Polypore, Berkeley's Polypore, Umbrella Polypore
habitat_notes: At the base of mature oaks and other hardwoods, often recurring on the same tree
range_notes: A large gray-brown rosette of many spoon-shaped fronds joined to a branched base beside mature hardwoods.
notes: Use young, fresh fronds and confirm the white pore surface. Similar rosette polypores differ in staining, color, and texture.

look_alikes: False Turkey Tail, Violet-toothed Polypore, Other Trametes species
habitat_notes: Overlapping shelves on dead hardwood logs, stumps, and branches
range_notes: Thin flexible fans with velvety multicolored bands above and a dense white pore surface below.
notes: Color bands alone do not identify turkey tail. Confirm a velvety cap and a true pore surface; medical extracts are not equivalent to a wild tea or supplement.

look_alikes: Amanita smithiana, Catathelasma species, Scaly Tricholoma species
habitat_notes: Deep duff under conifers, madrone, and other regional host trees
range_notes: A dense white pine mushroom with brown cap fibers, a sheathing ring, firm buried base, and a strong spicy odor.
notes: Amanita smithiana can resemble matsutake and cause kidney failure. This is not a beginner edible; use a qualified regional expert.

look_alikes: Destroying Angel, Yellow Stainer, Green-spored Parasol
habitat_notes: Lawns, pastures, playing fields, and other grassy soil
range_notes: A white grassland Agaricus whose free gills mature from pink to chocolate brown and whose base has no volva.
notes: White lawn mushrooms are a high-consequence identification problem. Dig the entire base and rule out deadly Amanita and yellow-staining Agaricus.

look_alikes: Devil's Urn, Pig's Ear, Other Craterellus species
habitat_notes: Leaf litter in mature broadleaf and mixed forest
range_notes: A thin charcoal funnel that is hollow to the base, with a smooth to faintly wrinkled gray outer surface and no gills.
notes: Dark cup fungi and regional Craterellus species require comparison. Confirm the thin hollow trumpet and smooth outer surface.

look_alikes: False Saffron Milk Cap, Woolly Milk Cap, Jack-o'-lantern
habitat_notes: Soil beneath pines, including plantations in introduced ranges
range_notes: An orange pine-associated milk cap with concentric cap zones, orange latex, and green staining where damaged.
notes: The deliciosus group contains regional species with different ranges and flavors. Confirm latex color, staining, gills, and host tree.

look_alikes: Meadow Mushroom, Paddy Straw Mushroom, Green Russula species
habitat_notes: Soil near oaks and other host trees in native and introduced ranges
range_notes: A deadly olive, bronze, yellow, or pale Amanita with free white gills, a ring, white spores, and a buried sack-like volva.
notes: Potentially fatal. If ingestion is possible, contact a poison center immediately and do not wait for symptoms.

look_alikes: Shaggy Parasol, Meadow Mushroom, Amanita species
habitat_notes: Lawns, parks, golf courses, and grassy disturbed soil
range_notes: A large lawn parasol with brown cap scales, a movable ring, and gills that turn gray-green as its green spores mature.
notes: Poisonous and capable of causing severe vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Never use cap shape alone to identify a parasol.

look_alikes: Golden Chanterelle, Rainbow Chanterelle, Chicken of the Woods
habitat_notes: Hardwood stumps, buried roots, and the bases of dead or declining trees
range_notes: A poisonous orange mushroom in dense wood-based clusters, with sharp true gills descending the stem.
notes: Poisonous. It is repeatedly mistaken for chanterelles; growth from wood and sharp true gills are critical differences.

look_alikes: Sheathed Woodtuft, Honey Mushroom, Mica Cap
habitat_notes: Decaying conifer and hardwood logs, stumps, and woody debris
range_notes: A small brown wood-growing mushroom with rusty gills and spores, a fragile ring zone, and potentially fatal amatoxins.
notes: Potentially fatal. Never eat little brown mushrooms from wood, and contact a poison center immediately after a possible ingestion.

look_alikes: Giant Puffball, Gem-studded Puffball, Amanita button
habitat_notes: Acidic soil, moss, path edges, and rotting wood near trees
range_notes: A firm yellow-brown ball with a thick cracked rind and a purple-black interior that distinguishes it from edible-stage puffballs.
notes: Poisonous. Cut every puffball-like mushroom vertically; earthballs develop a dark, firm center while edible-stage puffballs remain uniform white.

look_alikes: Shaggy Mane, Mica Cap, Other Ink Caps
habitat_notes: Buried wood, stumps, roots, lawns, and disturbed ground near hardwoods
range_notes: Smooth gray-brown clustered caps that dissolve into black ink and can trigger a severe alcohol reaction.
notes: Coprine can cause flushing, pounding heartbeat, nausea, and low blood pressure when alcohol is consumed around the same time.

look_alikes: King Bolete, Bitter Bolete, Red-pored Boletes
habitat_notes: High-elevation spruce and fir forest in the southern Rocky Mountains
range_notes: A high-elevation spruce bolete with a red-brown cap, white then yellow pores, and pale netting on a thick stem.
notes: Confirm pale stem reticulation, non-blue-staining pores, and local range. Avoid all red-pored or strongly blue-staining boletes as a beginner.

look_alikes: King Bolete, Bitter Bolete, Blue-staining Boletes
habitat_notes: Montane pine forest in western North America
range_notes: A western spring porcini with a brown cap, thick netted stem, white-to-yellow pores, and little or no blue staining.
notes: Western bolete names overlap. Confirm pine habitat, stem reticulation, pore color, bruising, and an expert-supported regional record.

look_alikes: Other Leccinum species, Rocky Mountain Porcini, Orange-capped Boletes
habitat_notes: Soil beneath aspen in western North America
range_notes: An orange-capped bolete under aspen, with pale pores and a white stem covered in dark scabers.
notes: Western Leccinum have caused gastrointestinal illness even after cooking. Regional identification and thorough cooking do not eliminate individual risk.

look_alikes: Artist's Conk, Ganoderma curtisii, Red-belted conks
habitat_notes: Dead or dying hemlock and other conifers in eastern North America
range_notes: A lacquered red-brown shelf on hemlock and other conifers, prized for tea and extracts rather than as a food mushroom.
notes: Woody and inedible as food. Health claims are not established; ask a clinician before using extracts, especially with blood-thinning medicines.

look_alikes: Birch burls, Tinder Fungus, Black knot
habitat_notes: Living and dying birch in boreal and cool temperate forests of the Northern Hemisphere
range_notes: A black, cracked, charcoal-like canker on birch trunks whose rusty orange interior is used for tea.
notes: Not a food mushroom. Heavy, long-term chaga tea use has been linked to oxalate kidney injury.

look_alikes: Black witch's butter, Brown cup fungi, Amber jelly roll
habitat_notes: Dead branches of elder, sycamore, and other hardwoods
range_notes: A rubbery, ear-shaped brown jelly fungus on dead hardwood, especially elder, eaten widely after cooking.
notes: Cook before eating. Soak dried wood ears briefly and refrigerate; long room-temperature soaking has caused severe bacterial toxin poisoning.

look_alikes: Coral fungi, Hen of the Woods, Other Sparassis species
habitat_notes: At the base of pines and other conifers, attached to roots
range_notes: A large cream rosette of flat, curly lobes at the base of conifers, easy to recognize and prized when fresh.
notes: Clean thoroughly and cook. Soft, discolored, or bitter specimens should be left.

look_alikes: Silver-blue milky, Blue webcaps, Faded indigo milk caps
habitat_notes: Oak and pine forests of eastern North America, Mexico, Central America, and parts of Asia
range_notes: A striking blue milk cap whose cut gills bleed blue latex that slowly stains green.
notes: Confirm the blue latex. Blue color alone can fade in older specimens.

look_alikes: Hexagonal-pored polypore, Other scaly polypores, Chicken of the Woods
habitat_notes: Living and dead hardwoods such as elm, maple, and box elder
range_notes: A large spring polypore with feathery brown scales, big angular pores, and a fresh watermelon-rind smell.
notes: Only young, tender edges are worth eating. Tough, older shelves are indigestible.

look_alikes: Chicken of the Woods, Red-belted conks, Bleeding polypores
habitat_notes: Trunks of oak and sweet chestnut
range_notes: A red, tongue-shaped bracket on oak and chestnut whose marbled flesh oozes red juice like raw meat.
notes: Sour and acidic; soak or cook, and avoid old, soft specimens.

look_alikes: Deadly Galerina, Red-hot milk cap, Other small brown milk caps
habitat_notes: Rotting wood and debris under oaks and conifers along the Pacific coast of North America
range_notes: A small orange-brown Pacific coast milk cap with watery latex and a maple-syrup aroma that intensifies when dried.
notes: Small brown mushrooms on wood include deadly Galerina. Confirm the watery latex and the aroma on every specimen.

look_alikes: False Chanterelle, Jack-o'-lantern, Woolly chanterelle
habitat_notes: Douglas-fir and western hemlock forests of the Pacific Northwest
range_notes: The common golden chanterelle of the Pacific Northwest, with blunt, forked false gills and a pinkish tone.
notes: Rule out false chanterelles and jack-o'-lanterns, which have true blade-like gills.

look_alikes: Scarlet Waxcap, Jack-o'-lantern, Red Russula species
habitat_notes: Soil and moss in oak and mixed hardwood forests of eastern North America
range_notes: A small, brilliant red-pink chanterelle of eastern North American hardwood forests.
notes: Small red mushrooms include waxcaps and other species. Confirm blunt ridges rather than true gills.

look_alikes: Deadly Webcap, Golden trumpet, False Chanterelle
habitat_notes: Moss, rotting wood, and needle litter in wet conifer forests
range_notes: A slender brown-capped chanterelle relative with a hollow yellow stem and gray forked ridges, fruiting late into winter.
notes: Small brown mushrooms with true gills, including deadly webcaps, grow in the same moss. Check for hollow stems and blunt ridges.

look_alikes: Violet webcaps, Lilac fibrecap, Amethyst Deceiver
habitat_notes: Leaf litter, compost heaps, and woodland edges
range_notes: A lilac-violet mushroom of autumn leaf litter and compost with a fruity smell and a pinkish-buff spore print.
notes: Always take a spore print: violet webcaps have rusty-brown spores and some are dangerous. Cook thoroughly; some people react even to cooked blewits.

look_alikes: Green-spored Parasol, Stinking Dapperling, Shaggy Parasol
habitat_notes: Grassland, meadows, and open woodland edges
range_notes: A towering meadow mushroom with a scaly brown cap up to 30 cm, a snakeskin-patterned stem, and a movable double ring.
notes: Confirm a white spore print and a movable ring. Small Lepiota species with similar scales can be deadly.

look_alikes: Green-spored Parasol, Parasol Mushroom, Brown parasol
habitat_notes: Conifer litter, gardens, compost, and woodland edges
range_notes: A shaggy-scaled parasol of conifer litter and compost whose cut flesh stains saffron then reddish brown.
notes: Causes gastrointestinal upset in some people. The green-spored parasol is similar; take a spore print every time.

look_alikes: Deadly Galerina, Sulphur Tuft, Jack-o'-lantern
habitat_notes: Stumps, roots, and living trees in hardwood and mixed forests
range_notes: Dense clusters of honey-colored caps on wood and roots, linked by black bootlace strands under bark.
notes: Always cook thoroughly; raw or undercooked honey mushrooms cause vomiting. Deadly Galerina grows on the same wood.

look_alikes: Deadly Galerina, Sulphur Tuft, Sheathed Woodtuft
habitat_notes: Dead or dying hardwood, especially elm, willow, and ash
range_notes: A cold-season cluster of sticky orange-brown caps on dead hardwood, with a velvety dark stem.
notes: Deadly Galerina grows on wood in the same cold months. Check for a white spore print and the absence of a ring.

look_alikes: Ringed Conecap, Yellow Stainer, Other Stropharia
habitat_notes: Wood chips, straw, garden beds, and rich disturbed ground
range_notes: A large burgundy mushroom of wood chips and gardens with a ridged cogwheel ring and purple-black gills.
notes: Take a spore print. Other mulch mushrooms, including Agaricus and Pholiotina, grow in the same beds.

look_alikes: Bitter Bolete, King Bolete, Red-cracked boletes
habitat_notes: Conifer and mixed forests on acidic soil
range_notes: A chestnut-brown bolete of conifer woods whose cream pores bruise blue when pressed.
notes: Avoid boletes with red or orange pores and any with a bitter taste. Cook thoroughly.

look_alikes: Weeping bolete, Peppery bolete, Other Suillus
habitat_notes: Under pines, including planted pines in the Southern Hemisphere
range_notes: A slimy brown pine bolete with a prominent purplish ring, now common in pine plantations worldwide.
notes: Peel the slimy cap skin before cooking; the slime causes digestive upset in some people.

look_alikes: Strobilomyces confusus, Shaggy Amanita, Scaly tooth fungi
habitat_notes: Oak and mixed hardwood forests
range_notes: A shaggy gray-and-black bolete that looks like a pine cone, with gray pores bruising red then black.
notes: Edible but mediocre. Cook well, and confirm it is a bolete with pores.

look_alikes: Bitter Bolete, King Bolete, Devil's Bolete
habitat_notes: Pine and spruce forests on acidic soil
range_notes: A porcini with a wine-red to mahogany cap, found under pines and spruce across Europe.
notes: Rule out bitter and red-pored boletes. Taste a tiny raw piece and spit it out; bitterness means bitter bolete.

look_alikes: Bitter Bolete, King Bolete, Pine Bolete
habitat_notes: Oak, beech, and other broadleaf woodland
range_notes: An early porcini with a pale, often cracked brown cap and a fine white net over the entire stem.
notes: Rule out the bitter bolete, which has a dark net and pinkish pores.

look_alikes: Aspen Bolete, Red-capped scaber stalk, Bitter Bolete
habitat_notes: With birch, in heath, woods, and parks
range_notes: A bright orange bolete under birch with a scabrous, black-flecked stem and flesh that darkens when cut.
notes: Cook thoroughly. Raw or undercooked Leccinum has caused gastrointestinal illness, and some North American orange Leccinum are implicated in poisonings.

look_alikes: Bitter Bolete, Other brown scaber stalks, Bay Bolete
habitat_notes: With birch in woods, heath, and parks
range_notes: A common brown-capped bolete of birch with a white stem covered in dark scabers.
notes: Cook thoroughly, and discard old, soft caps. Some people react to Leccinum even when cooked.

look_alikes: Deadly Fibrecap, Livid Pinkgill, Fool's Funnel
habitat_notes: Grassland edges, hedgerows, and woodland margins, often in rings
range_notes: A stocky white spring mushroom of grassland and hedgerows with crowded white gills and a strong mealy smell.
notes: The deadly fibrecap and livid pinkgill also fruit in spring. Confirm a white spore print, mealy smell, and no reddening.

look_alikes: Fool's Funnel, Ringed Conecap, Other lawn mushrooms
habitat_notes: Lawns, pastures, and short grass
range_notes: A small tan lawn mushroom with widely spaced gills and a tough, bendable stem, growing in rings.
notes: The fool's funnel grows in the same lawns and is poisonous. Check gill spacing and attachment on every specimen.

look_alikes: Yellow Stainer, European Destroying Angel, Meadow Mushroom
habitat_notes: Pastures, meadows, and grassy verges
range_notes: A large white grassland Agaricus with an aniseed smell, a cogwheel ring, and gills maturing to chocolate brown.
notes: Destroying angels are white with white gills and a volva. The yellow stainer bruises chrome yellow and smells of ink.

look_alikes: Lilac bonnet, Lilac fibrecap, Violet webcaps
habitat_notes: Leaf and needle litter in broadleaf and conifer woods
range_notes: A slender, intensely violet woodland mushroom with thick, widely spaced gills that fades when dry.
notes: It can accumulate arsenic from some soils. Lilac bonnet and lilac fibrecap are toxic lookalikes.

look_alikes: Panther Cap, Gray spotted amanita, Death Cap
habitat_notes: Broadleaf and conifer woodland
range_notes: A reddish-brown Amanita with pale warts whose flesh and bruises turn pinkish red, especially at the stem base.
notes: An Amanita. It must be thoroughly cooked, and the panther cap is a dangerous lookalike. North American blushers are separate species.

look_alikes: Fly Agaric, Death Cap, American Caesar's Mushroom
habitat_notes: Oak and chestnut woods of southern Europe and North Africa
range_notes: A brilliant orange Amanita with yellow gills and a large white sac volva, prized in southern Europe since Roman times.
notes: It is an Amanita. Unopened eggs resemble deadly death cap eggs; cut vertically and confirm yellow internal gills.

look_alikes: Fly Agaric, Yellow patches, Death Cap
habitat_notes: Oak and pine forests of eastern North America
range_notes: A red-orange Amanita of eastern North America with a striate cap margin, yellow gills, and a white sac volva.
notes: An Amanita. Confirm yellow gills and stem and the white sac volva, and cut eggs vertically.

look_alikes: Death Cap, The Sickener, Other Russula
habitat_notes: Broadleaf woods, especially beech and oak
range_notes: A variably colored Russula in violet, green, and gray whose gills are flexible rather than brittle.
notes: Green-tinged Russulas can be confused with the death cap. Confirm no ring and no volva.

look_alikes: The Sickener, Other red Russula, Charcoal Burner
habitat_notes: Conifer and mixed forests
range_notes: A red to purple-brown Russula that smells of shrimp or crab with age and bruises yellow-brown.
notes: Red Russulas include acrid, toxic species. Confirm the fishy odor, brown staining, and mild taste.

look_alikes: Woolly Milk Cap, Corrugated milk cap, Red-hot milk cap
habitat_notes: Hardwood and mixed forests
range_notes: An orange-brown milk cap that releases abundant white latex staining brown, with a fishy smell.
notes: Other orange milk caps release acrid latex. Confirm mild, abundant white latex that stains brown.

look_alikes: Woolly chanterelle, Black Trumpet, Violet corals
habitat_notes: Old conifer forests, often in deep needle litter
range_notes: A purple, club-shaped relative of chanterelles with a wrinkled, veined underside, declining in parts of Europe.
notes: Protected or red-listed in several European countries. The scaly vase chanterelle is a toxic lookalike.

look_alikes: Bear's head tooth, Lion's Mane, Coral fungi
habitat_notes: Fallen logs and stumps of beech, birch, maple, and other hardwoods
range_notes: A white, branching fungus on dead hardwood with rows of short spines hanging from every branch.
notes: Harvest only fresh, white specimens; yellowing ones are bitter.

look_alikes: Sulphur Tuft, Oyster Mushroom, Golden Pholiota
habitat_notes: Dead elm and other hardwoods; escaped from cultivation in North America
range_notes: Bright yellow clusters of oyster mushrooms on hardwood; native to East Asia and invasive in North American forests.
notes: Check host wood and gill attachment, and confirm the white to pale lilac spore print.

look_alikes: Deadly Galerina, Brittlestems, Common Ink Cap
habitat_notes: Stumps, buried roots, and dead hardwood, often in towns
range_notes: Small tawny bell-shaped caps sprinkled with glittering granules, in dense clusters on wood.
notes: Very perishable; cook within hours. Small brown mushrooms on wood also include deadly Galerina.

look_alikes: Livid Pinkgill, Destroying Angel, Puffballs
habitat_notes: Near rotting hardwood and buried wood in eastern North America
range_notes: Whitish, lumpy masses beside gray gilled Entoloma mushrooms, formed where Entoloma and honey mushrooms interact.
notes: Only the lumpy form is widely eaten. Cut every lump: it must have uniform flesh without internal gills.

look_alikes: Deadly Galerina, Honey Mushroom, Sulphur Tuft
habitat_notes: Stumps and logs of broadleaf trees
range_notes: A clustered brown mushroom on stumps with two-toned drying caps and a scaly stem below the ring.
notes: The deadly Galerina marginata is almost identical. Most experts advise beginners to avoid this species entirely.

look_alikes: Smith's Amanita, Western Matsutake, Tricholoma focale
habitat_notes: Red pine and other pines, in poor, sandy soils
range_notes: A prized, spicy-smelling mushroom of red pine forests in East Asia and northern Europe with a sheathing ring.
notes: Kidney-toxic Amanita smithiana and other white mushrooms can resemble matsutake. Confirm the spicy odor and the lack of a volva.

look_alikes: Darwin's fungus, Empty galls, Other orange fungi
habitat_notes: Branches of southern beech (Nothofagus) in Chile and Argentina
range_notes: Golden, pitted balls that grow from galls on southern beech branches in Patagonia.
notes: Collect only fresh, firm balls, and leave galls intact.

look_alikes: Livid Pinkgill, Amanita, Other Pluteus
habitat_notes: Rotting logs, stumps, sawdust, and buried wood
range_notes: A brown-capped mushroom on dead wood with free white gills that turn pink and a pink spore print.
notes: Confirm pink spores and free gills. Some Pluteus contain psychoactive compounds, and Entoloma are toxic.

look_alikes: Ramaria corals, Coral Tooth Fungus, Clavulina corals
habitat_notes: Rotting logs of aspen, willow, poplar, and other hardwoods
range_notes: A candelabra-like coral fungus on rotting hardwood, each branch ending in a small crown of points.
notes: Many corals grow on soil and some cause digestive upset. Confirm growth on wood and crown-shaped tips.

look_alikes: The Blusher, Gray spotted amanita, Fly Agaric
habitat_notes: Broadleaf and conifer woodland
range_notes: A brown Amanita with pure white warts, a striate margin, and a rimmed bulb, more toxic than the fly agaric.
notes: Poisonous. Contains ibotenic acid and muscimol, causing confusion, agitation, and seizures. Seek poison-center advice after any ingestion.

look_alikes: Horse Mushroom, Puffballs, St George's Mushroom
habitat_notes: Acidic woodland with birch, pine, and spruce in northern and central Europe
range_notes: A pure white, deadly Amanita of northern European woods with a shaggy stem and a large sac-like volva.
notes: Potentially fatal. Contains amatoxins that survive cooking. Contact a poison center immediately after any possible ingestion.

look_alikes: Meadow Mushroom, Springtime amanita, Puffballs
habitat_notes: With oaks, especially coast live oak, in California and neighboring states
range_notes: A white, deadly Amanita of California and the Pacific coast that fruits in late winter and spring under oaks.
notes: Potentially fatal. Contains amatoxins. Contact a poison center immediately after any possible ingestion.

look_alikes: Western Matsutake, Matsutake, Catathelasma
habitat_notes: Conifer and mixed forests of the Pacific Northwest
range_notes: A shaggy white Amanita of Pacific Northwest conifer forests that causes delayed kidney failure.
notes: Poisonous. Causes delayed kidney injury that can require dialysis. It is often mistaken for matsutake.

look_alikes: Death Cap, European Destroying Angel, Panther Cap
habitat_notes: Broadleaf and conifer woods on acidic soil
range_notes: A pale lemon to white Amanita with a large rimmed bulb and a raw-potato smell, easily confused with the death cap.
notes: Not a food mushroom. Its main danger is confusion with the death cap and other deadly Amanita.

look_alikes: Honey Mushroom, Conifer tuft, Sheathed Woodtuft
habitat_notes: Stumps and dead wood of broadleaf and conifer trees
range_notes: Dense clusters of sulphur-yellow caps with greenish gills on stumps, bitter tasting and poisonous.
notes: Poisonous; causes vomiting and diarrhea, and severe poisonings are reported. Do not confuse with honey mushrooms or woodtufts.

look_alikes: Fairy Ring Mushroom, The miller, St George's Mushroom
habitat_notes: Lawns, pastures, and grassland, often in rings
range_notes: A small, frosty-white lawn mushroom with decurrent gills that contains muscarine and grows beside fairy rings.
notes: Poisonous. Muscarine causes sweating, salivation, tears, and slowed heart rate. Seek medical care after ingestion.

look_alikes: Yellowfoot, Golden Chanterelle, Other Cortinarius
habitat_notes: Wet, mossy conifer forests in northern Europe and North America
range_notes: An orange-brown webcap of wet conifer forests containing orellanine, which causes delayed kidney failure.
notes: Potentially fatal. Kidney damage may not show for days to weeks after eating. Seek emergency care after any possible ingestion.

look_alikes: Golden Chanterelle, Deadly Webcap, Other Cortinarius
habitat_notes: Oak and beech woods in warm parts of Europe
range_notes: A tawny-orange webcap of European broadleaf woods whose toxin, orellanine, destroys the kidneys.
notes: Potentially fatal. Symptoms can be delayed by days to weeks. Seek emergency care after any possible ingestion.

look_alikes: Milk caps, Velvet roll-rim, Saffron Milk Cap
habitat_notes: Woods, heath, and parks, especially with birch
range_notes: A brown mushroom with a strongly inrolled rim and soft gills that bruise brown, once eaten but now known to be dangerous.
notes: Poisonous and potentially fatal. Repeated meals can trigger an immune reaction that destroys red blood cells.

look_alikes: Lurid boletes, Other red-pored boletes, King Bolete
habitat_notes: Oak and beech woods on calcareous soil in Europe
range_notes: A stout pale-capped bolete with red pores and a red-netted stem, found on chalky soils under oak and beech.
notes: Poisonous. Causes severe vomiting and diarrhea. Avoid boletes with red or orange pores unless expertly identified.

look_alikes: King Bolete, Bay Bolete, Summer Bolete
habitat_notes: Conifer and hardwood forests, often on acidic soil
range_notes: A king-bolete lookalike with pinkish pores, a dark net on the stem, and a taste so bitter it ruins a meal.
notes: Not toxic, but one specimen can make a whole dish inedible.

look_alikes: Beechwood sickener, Shrimp Russula, Other red Russula
habitat_notes: Wet, mossy conifer woods, often with sphagnum
range_notes: A scarlet Russula of wet conifer woods with pure white gills and a burning, acrid taste.
notes: Poisonous raw. Causes vomiting and diarrhea.

look_alikes: Saffron Milk Cap, Downy milk cap, Weeping Milk Cap
habitat_notes: With birch
range_notes: A pinkish, zoned milk cap with a woolly, bearded margin and acrid white latex, found with birch.
notes: Poisonous raw. Traditional processing in some countries does not make it safe for casual use.

look_alikes: Meadow Mushroom, Horse Mushroom, Destroying Angel
habitat_notes: Gardens, parks, hedgerows, and woodland edges
range_notes: A white Agaricus that instantly stains chrome yellow when scratched, especially at the cut stem base, and smells of ink.
notes: Poisonous. The most common cause of Agaricus poisoning. Always cut the stem base and smell the flesh.

look_alikes: Golden Chanterelle, Jack-o'-lantern, Pacific Golden Chanterelle
habitat_notes: Conifer litter and rotting wood
range_notes: An orange mushroom with thin, crowded, repeatedly forked true gills, often mistaken for a chanterelle.
notes: Not recommended; it can cause digestive upset. Its main danger is teaching the wrong chanterelle features.

look_alikes: Oyster Mushroom, Angel Wings, Other Omphalotus
habitat_notes: Dead and dying trees and stumps in southern Australia, including eucalypts and pines
range_notes: A creamy, fan-shaped Australian mushroom that glows green in the dark and causes vomiting when eaten.
notes: Poisonous. Contains illudin toxins that cause severe vomiting. Often mistaken for oyster mushrooms.

look_alikes: Deadly dapperlings, Parasol Mushroom, Fairy Ring Mushroom
habitat_notes: Disturbed ground, lawns, gardens, and woodland edges
range_notes: A small white Lepiota with a brown center and concentric scales, a fragile ring, and a rubbery chemical smell.
notes: Poisonous. Several small Lepiota contain deadly amatoxins; treat every small Lepiota as potentially lethal.

look_alikes: St George's Mushroom, The miller, Other fibrecaps
habitat_notes: Beech and other broadleaf woods, parks, and path edges, often on chalk
range_notes: A cream fibrous-capped spring mushroom that reddens with age and has caused fatal muscarine poisoning.
notes: Potentially fatal. Contains high levels of muscarine. Often confused with St George's mushroom.

look_alikes: Psilocybe species, Fairy Ring Mushroom, Deadly Galerina
habitat_notes: Lawns, wood chips, mulch, and gardens
range_notes: A small brown lawn and mulch mushroom with a movable ring and rusty spores that contains deadly amatoxins.
notes: Potentially fatal to people and pets. Contains amatoxins. Contact a poison center immediately after any ingestion.

look_alikes: St George's Mushroom, Clouded agaric, The miller
habitat_notes: Broadleaf woods, often on clay or chalk
range_notes: A large pale gray-buff mushroom with yellowish gills that turn pink, a mealy smell, and a pink spore print.
notes: Poisonous. Causes severe, prolonged vomiting and diarrhea and has caused hospitalizations.

look_alikes: Sulphur knight, Aspen knight, Other yellow Tricholoma
habitat_notes: Sandy pine forests
range_notes: A yellow knight mushroom of sandy pine forests once widely eaten, now linked to fatal muscle breakdown.
notes: Poisonous. Repeated meals have caused rhabdomyolysis and deaths in France and Poland.

look_alikes: Morel, Half-free morel, False Morel
habitat_notes: With cottonwood, aspen, and poplar along streams
range_notes: An early-spring morel lookalike whose wrinkled cap hangs free from the top of a cotton-filled stem.
notes: Not recommended. It has caused gastrointestinal upset and loss of coordination, especially after large or repeated meals.

look_alikes: Black elfin saddle, False Morel, Early False Morel
habitat_notes: Woodland paths and broadleaf woods
range_notes: A pale, saddle-shaped cup fungus on a deeply furrowed, chambered stem, toxic raw.
notes: Toxic raw and not recommended even cooked. Related species contain gyromitrin-like compounds.

look_alikes: Oyster Mushroom, Ghost Fungus, Crepidotus
habitat_notes: Rotting conifer logs, especially hemlock
range_notes: Thin, pure white, ear-shaped caps on rotting conifer wood, once eaten and now linked to fatal brain illness.
notes: Poisonous. Linked to fatal acute encephalopathy, especially in people with kidney disease.

look_alikes: Hemlock Reishi, Tinder Fungus, Red-belted conks
habitat_notes: Dead and living hardwoods, occasionally conifers
range_notes: A large, woody, perennial bracket with a dull crusty top and a white pore surface that bruises brown when scratched.
notes: Woody and not a food mushroom.

look_alikes: Tinder Fungus, Chaga, Other white brackets
habitat_notes: Dead and dying birch
range_notes: A smooth, pale, kidney-shaped bracket that grows only on birch, carried by Ötzi the Iceman 5,300 years ago.
notes: Tough and bitter; not a food mushroom.

look_alikes: Artist's Conk, Willow bracket, Birch Polypore
habitat_notes: Birch, beech, and other hardwoods
range_notes: A gray, hoof-shaped perennial bracket on birch and beech, used for millennia to carry fire.
notes: Woody and not a food mushroom.

look_alikes: Stalked scarlet cups, Orange Peel Fungus, Eyelash cup
habitat_notes: Fallen hardwood sticks, often buried in moss or leaf litter
range_notes: A brilliant scarlet cup fungus on mossy fallen sticks in winter and early spring.
notes: Not treated as food here; collect for study only.

look_alikes: Scarlet Elf Cup, Spring orange peel, Eyelash cup
habitat_notes: Bare or disturbed soil, paths, and roadsides
range_notes: A bright orange cup fungus on bare, disturbed soil that looks like discarded orange peel.
notes: Small and fragile. Confirm it is on soil, not wood, and does not stain blue-green.

look_alikes: Death Cap, Dog stinkhorn, Puffballs
habitat_notes: Woodland and gardens with buried wood
range_notes: A white spongy stalk topped with foul-smelling olive slime that hatches from a buried egg and attracts flies.
notes: Its egg stage can resemble a deadly Amanita egg. Cut any egg-like mushroom vertically.

look_alikes: Barometer earthstar, Other earthstars, Puffballs
habitat_notes: Leaf litter in broadleaf and conifer woods
range_notes: A puffball whose outer skin splits into star-shaped rays, often with a saucer-like collar under the spore sac.
notes: Not a food mushroom.

look_alikes: Crimson waxcap, Blackening waxcap, Cinnabar Chanterelle
habitat_notes: Old grasslands, lawns, and pastures that have not been fertilized
range_notes: A brilliant scarlet waxcap of old, unfertilized grasslands, where it signals valuable habitat.
notes: Leave it. Waxcap grasslands are declining and protected in some regions.

look_alikes: Orange jelly spot, Black witch's butter, Wood Ear
habitat_notes: Dead hardwood branches, often still attached to the tree
range_notes: A bright yellow, lobed jelly fungus on dead hardwood branches in cool, wet weather.
notes: Bland and gelatinous. Confirm a hardwood host.
